For more than forty years, under five emperors, he told the Heian court what the stars meant, and the most powerful men in Japan listened. But was Abe no Seimei really a sorcerer who commanded spirits, or a careful government official whose greatest power was trust? We separate the documented man from a thousand years of legend.

Your reporter: Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent whose grandfather's brass pocket watch carries him to a single day in Japan's past. He can watch and speak, but he can never change what happens.

scenes.narration: I'm Tokio Kamiya, a former newspaper correspondent. My grandfather, a Kyoto clockmaker, left me a brass pocket watch, and it carries me to any moment in Japan's past, one day at a time. I can watch and speak, but I can never change a thing. At dawn, I walk the main avenue of Heian-kyo, a capital founded in 794 and laid out with the sky in mind. Its planners believed that mountains, rivers and compass directions carry invisible power, and the court here runs on omens. A comet, a fire or a crow at the wrong gate can change the calendar of state. To read such signs, the court employs salaried officials, not wandering mystics: the Onmyoryo, the Bureau of Yin and Yang.

scenes.narration: Later that morning, I'm shown into the Bureau's office, as quiet as any ministry. The Bureau practices three main crafts: astronomy, the calendar and divination. Astronomers watch the heavens and report anything unusual. Calendar masters calculate the days and the months. Diviners judge which days are lucky for a journey, a wedding or a ceremony, and which ones to avoid. Courtiers consult them the way we might consult a government office. And into this world, according to tradition in the year 921, a boy named Abe no Seimei was born.

Each night, a duty astronomer watches the stars from a platform, noting the planets, the comets and the path of the moon, while a colleague records each reading. Any reading must be exact. A comet or an eclipse is not scenery; it is a message addressed to the emperor, and misreading it could shake a reign. The work is slow, cold and solitary. I suspect it teaches him that whoever interprets the sky holds a quiet power.
